text: This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Farai Chideya in for Ed Gordon.

On today's roundtable we examine the lawsuits rolling in as New Orleans      dries out.  We'll look at the economic impact Hurricane Katrina is having      on the various cities that evacuees now call home.  And we'll hear what      our panelists think about a new BET documentary on local and federal      government response to the disaster.

Joining us now from member station WRNI in Providence, Rhode Island, is      Glenn Loury.  He's professor of economics at Brown University.  At our      Washington, DC, headquarters, Jeffrey Johnson, host and producer of the      "Cousin Jeff Chronicles" on BET.  Jeff has been to New Orleans twice and      visited evacuees with rapper Kanye West.  And finally, George Curry,      editor in chief of the National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service in Maryland.
Welcome to all of you.
Good morning.

So let me just jump in on the issue of these lawsuits.  There      was the very well noted case of the deaths in a nursing home, residents      just left there to die.  Are these lawsuits just?  Let me start with you,      George.  Are we going to see a lot of litigiousness, and is it justified?

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Of course we're going to see a lot of lawsuits.  You're going      to have arguments about what really caused the damage, the floods or the      hurricane.  And people lost a lot of money, a lot of houses, a lot of      people, a lot of businesses. And so that's where we saw these kinds of      disputes, and I think a lot of them will end up in court.  I think the      difference, though--the major difference is when you file a civil court      case vs. a criminal case is that the standard of proof is actually lower.      You just have to rely on the preponderance of evidence as opposed to a      stricter standard, so I think that they'll be easier to win but I think      it'll be very, very difficult, with respect--difficult, and we can expect      to see a lot of lawsuits.

Glenn, I don't know whether you've heard about the fact that      the state of Mississippi is suing insurers to make sure the people who      didn't have flood insurance actually get their claims paid.
No, I didn't know that.

Yeah, I find that very interesting.  Do you think that that      strategy is wise for the state to actually sue the insurance companies?      Is that the only way that some people are going to get their claims paid?

Well, I don't know enough about the facts to really have an      opinion on what the state's doing, but I will say this.  There's a huge      amount of money at stake, and those insurance policies did have      specifications. Obviously there's going to then be struggle between      claimants and the insurance companies each trying to do the best for      themselves in the circumstances.  My instinct is that the state should      stay out of that and that courts should interpret those contracts when      disputes arise.  There could be many billions of dollars involved for the      insurance companies, but the politics of the situation probably are going      to militate in favor of the politicians trying to get as much for the      people as they can.
And, Jeff...
And, Farai, if I      can interject.
Yes, Jeff.

I like what the state is doing.  I think that there are a      large number of poor folks who will not get any benefits otherwise.  And      I think--I agree.  I think that there will be obviously some      overpoliticization of this process.  But I do think that there are those      who, even if it's a small claim, are going to be able to get benefits      that otherwise they wouldn't have got if the state didn't get involved.

Well, let me just say this.  I don't want to argue.  I      mean, I want those people to get benefits, too.  The question is whether      or not it's the insurance companies that are responsible to give them,      outside of the terms of contracts, or whether it's the general public who      ought to pay the freight if we want to see people get, you know,      benefits.

Well, Glenn, let me give you a very personal example.  My uncle      actually owned a multi-unit apartment complex in New Orleans.  And when      he went in for insurance, he was told he didn't need flood insurance      because his place was in the French Quarter and it wasn't on the flood      plain.  Now they're telling him, `You don't have flood insurance so we're      not going to pay your claim.'  What...
Yeah.

What should happen?  And he's going to go to court and try to      figure it out, you know, and obviously this is one very specific, very      personal example to me.  But in a case like that, where people, on the      recommendation of insurers, didn't get the kind of insurance that would      have protected them, what should happen in a legal sense?

I don't know.  My instinct is probably in case like that,      the guy has a claim, you know.  But what--all cases are not the same, and      that's why I think courts probably ought to adjudicate these disputes as      opposed to, you know, a kind of blanket resolution being imposed on all      the cases by a statute.

Well, let me turn back to you, Jeff.  There was a documentary      on BET yesterday and, of course, you do your "Cousin Jeff Chronicles" for      BET.  It was called "Answering the Call:  A BET News SOS Update."  It      talked about everything from the role that race played the disaster to      some very moving personal stories of people who sacrificed to save their      families.  What is the role of black media now that the immediate tragedy      is over but the resettlement will continue?

Well, I think that clearly there are more stories than      there is time to tell them.  And the black media, with every resource      that it has, I think is going to have a responsibility to tell some of      the stories that the major media will not tell.  I think it's going to be      very interesting how this discussion on race continues to play out.  I      think there needs to be a real microscope or magnifying glass at least      placed on so many of the areas that haven't gotten media attention.      There've been so many cities and towns in the state of Mississippi and      Louisiana that have, in many cases, been overshadowed by the tragedy that      took place in New Orleans.  And so I think that the media attention that      can be placed on those areas is necessary to ensure that public opinion      and public outcry is made for those people that are suffering, in many      cases, as much as those who have been displaced from New Orleans.  And I      think that's one of the things that has to happen.

I think additionally the media has to be involved in just the ongoing      political issues that are going to take place around the president, all      of his promises, that in many cases many believe he has no ability to      deliver on, especially if we remain in Iraq.  And so I think that there's      so many stories that have come out of this tragedy that the black press      needs to be very focused on providing some of those stories that we may      not see on CBS, NBC and FOX News.

Let me just ask you one follow-up.  BET is undergoing some      restructuring.  Reginald Hudlin was brought in to revamp programming.      The BET News is, you know, boasting that it will have a new look on      October 3rd, coming up.  Some people have been extremely happy with BET's      response to this disaster.  Other people said, `Why did you keep playing      all those music videos?  Why didn't we have wall-to-wall, 24-hour      coverage?'  Now I know it's an awkward thing to ask you, since you're      working for BET, but do you think that the channel or other      African-American channels should have just turned themselves into news      outlets and gone wall-to-wall, 24 hours as at least the initial disaster      was unfolding?

As a citizen and somebody that's concerned with the issue,      as I've been down to the Gulf on three occasions now, I thought it would      have been fantastic if those networks did that.  As somebody that has      some insight on the behind-the-scenes piece, I understand that that's a      more difficult proposition, once you start talking about resources to do      that.  I think BET was caught in a very difficult place, being in the      middle of restructuring and not having the pieces in place to be able to      do that.

However, I think BET could have done a better job than it did of      providing updates, of providing information, of ensuring that people were      on the ground to tell the stories that otherwise have not been told.  And      I don't know if any of our networks, TV1, the Black Family Channel or      BET, from a television perspective, had the resources to be able to do      that.  That's why I think your earlier question is even more important,      about how it's going to be handled from this point, because while the      bulk of the emergency piece is over, there are going to be real stories      from a media perspective that can--that have to be told for the next year      at least.  And I'm hoping that BET in its restructuring has the ability      and the wherewithal to focus on the stories that are important so that      people who don't get their news from anywhere else can get it.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Let me interject here.
George.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: I used to be editor of Emerge magazine, which was owned by      BET. And, of course, was on "Lead Stories" for seven years with Ed      Gordon.  And let's just go ahead and cut to the chase.  BET has      downsized.  It's de-emphasized its news programs, its public affairs      programs, and I used to be one who defended it because even with the rump      shaking, they had "BET Tonight," they had "Teen Summit," they had "Lead      Stories" and then recently had the news.  They have basically gotten rid      of all those programs.  I don't care how they try to repackage it and      say, `We're going to have news updates,' there has been a de-emphasis of      news on BET.
No, but, George, since Reggie has come in...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: He's over entertainment.  He's not over news.  He's over      entertainment.
But...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: He's president of entertainment.

I understand that, but as someone that's inside now, I      understand how the restructuring's taking place.  I am the last person      that's attempting to defend what BET has not done up unto this point in      time. However, I am aware of at least three public affairs news programs      that are slated since Reggie has come in.  So I'm not talking about the      news...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Well, I hope you're right.
...bullets or the hourly updates.  And I think we've got to      hold Reggie to the fire, so he's not just going to be      ...(unintelligible).

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Well, let me just follow up.  I mean, you know, I hear this      announcement, but all I'm seeing is with the news--and I hope you're      absolutely right, that there will be good news, but right now what I see      is they took the news off and said, `I'm going to have updates.'  They      had that 20 years ago, OK?  So we should never get to the point where we      have the de-emphasis of all these public affairs programs, so I'll be      watching very closely, and let's not forget that BET is not black only.      It's owned by Viacom.

Let me bring Glenn in on this.  You are a professor of      economics at Brown University.  George Curry, as he mentioned, used to be      editor of Emerge, which was acquired by BET and then closed.  Is there a      profit model for the news about something like Katrina, let alone by      black-run stations?  You know, there's been a de-emphasis in general of      news as a, you know, loss leader for these entertainment companies that      now own a lot of the news outlets.

Yeah, that's my impression.  I'm not by any means an expert      on the media market, but my sense is that the news is having a hard time      getting the resources inside these corporations that it needs to be done      properly across the board.  I wish that we had greater infrastructure to      bring a kind of sympathetic and humane portrayal of the lives of      African-Americans in the face of this disaster and otherwise into the      American media stream, because it's desperately needed to counter the      stigmatizing and stereotyping images and conceptions that are being      projected otherwise.  I hope that BET pulls its weight in that regard.

Let me ask you a follow-up economic question.  There was a poll      by The Washington Post and the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation.  It      found that fewer than half of the Katrina victims or evacuees living in      Houston want to go back to New Orleans.  Now what are the economic      ramifications or the political ramifications of the fact that some of the      people who were most vulnerable in the city just have no desire at this      point to go back?

Well, this is extremely interesting.  I did take note of      the results in that poll.  At the personal level, people thinking about      going back, I guess the question's going to be:  Go back to what exactly?      The communities that may have nurtured them before the disaster are no      longer there.  There aren't jobs, therefore then, and so forth.  On the      other hand, if you think about the politics of the siting of public      housing, in any big city in the United States, it's always extremely      contentious.  There's a reason why our big cities are dramatically      segregated by race and class.  And anyplace that large numbers of people      from the 9th Ward and other such communities in New Orleans are settled      are going to end up being different places than they had been before      those newcomers came.  The lines outside the gun shops in Baton Rouge      tell us something about the kind of backlash and the kind of politics      that we're going to be seeing played out in these communities.
Now let me get you in on...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: My theory is what you had earlier...
Go ahead, George.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: ...what you had earlier, a guest on, and that is you're      rushing people back there with all these contaminants still present in      the hopes that we're going to have a Mardi Gras early next year, just to      show that we're back.  I mean, there are too many dangers there, and I      think the mayor's getting ahead of himself.

Farai, I think also, and I'll be very quick, is that we      should question that poll.  I mean, I was in Houston and at the      Astrodome.  Most of the people that I talked to wanted to go back home.      And so I think we should be very careful, too, in some of these polls,      because there's going to be some maneuvering for developers to try to get      as much land as they can in New Orleans.  And I think we--and I don't      want to be a conspiracy theorist, but I think we have to be very careful      in those kind of polling numbers because there are people that don't know      anything but New Orleans and what they're getting in Baton Rouge and      Houston and other cities is not what they anticipated, is not at the      level that they need, and so they're not being treated in these other      cities so well that I can imagine them saying, `This is going to be my      new home.'

Jeff, let me follow up on that.  There was a big Los Angeles      Times article about real estate speculation in New Orleans.  You have      been there. You've seen what the city looks like.  What is your      worst-case scenario and best-case scenario for how some of the poorest      folks from New Orleans will fare in the new New Orleans in terms of real      estate development?

Well, first, I agree with George.  I think the proposition      of moving back in immediately is very dangerous where we don't know all      the contaminants that exist.  But I think from a real estate standpoint,      worst-case scenario, there's already Halliburton on the ground.  There      are already developers on the ground that are attempting to reshape what      the city looks like for the benefit of the rich.  We are--even right now      the poor are being pitted against the poor when you're seeing poor folks      battling against poor folks in Houston.

And so the question is, worst-case scenario, who's going to represent the      poorest of the poor in New Orleans as it relates to ensuring that      people's property is protected, especially those that didn't have      insurance, insuring that part of the city as it's redeveloped, the      portions that were so underdeveloped in the past?  And we know that New      Orleans is one of the poorest cities--large cities in the country.  Are      those developments that were sorely underdeveloped now going to be      developed in a way that is favorable to those who would live there?      Best-case scenario, the mayor is going to push for that kind of      protection, but I don't know if I believe that's going to happen.  I      really think we're going to be looking at worst-case scenario, which is a      mad dash for developers to try to get as much land as they can to turn it      into the new Gulf resort city that so many wish it could have been      before.
But, Glenn...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: Well, mayor appointed a commission, I think it's eight blacks      and eight whites...
George.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (National Newspaper Publishers Association News      Service)
text: ...that would actually decide the future of the city and help      plot where it's going.  And so you have that kind of balance and to have      that kind of power there, or you might see some dif--at least some fair      consideration.

And, Glenn, let me get you in on this whole question of what is      the best- and worst-case scenario from the perspective of what's the      mechanism? Right now you have a lot of people or a lot of agencies all      sort of wrangling for turf.  You have individual developers, individual      homeowners, federal, state and local government, non-governmental      agencies like all of the relief agencies, and as Jeff said, who is going      to look out for the interests of the poor folks?  Who should be?  You      know, in the kind of governmental and legal system that we have right      now, who does get to look out for the interest of people who may not have      means of their own?

I think this is a fundamental question.  I agree very much      with what Jeff said.  In my mind, the principle here has to be that this      is not just about property.  This is also about people and about their      relationships and their communities.  And the entitlement here is not      just the ownership of pieces of land or real estate, but it's also the      stake that individuals had in the city by virtue of having been a part of      the city.  So the politics of this has to be shaped by a conception in      New Orleans which is not just putting stuff back on the ground, but it's      also restoring--you know, it's also restoring the community and, if you      like, the kind of spiritual life of the city and the role that poor black      people played in the reality of New Orleans has somehow to be reflected.      And it's not going to be reflected if all you're talking about is who      owned what and who's going to be compensated for what they owned, because      those people didn't own that much.

All right.  We're going to have to leave it there.  That was      Glenn Loury, professor of economics at Brown University, joining us from      WRNI in Providence, Rhode Island.  And at Washington, DC's, headquarters,      Jeffrey Johnson, host and producer of the "Cousin Jeff Chronicles" on      BET.  Finally, George Curry, editor in chief of the National Newspaper      Publishers Association New Service in Maryland.  Thank you, gentlemen,      all for joining us.
Thank you, Farai.
Thank you.
You're listening to NEWS & NOTES from NPR News.

This is NEWS AND NOTES, I'm Ed Gordon. On today's ROUNDTABLE, President Bush vows that Iraqi troops will be in control of their country by the end of year and ready or not, here it comes, the bird flu.

speaker_label: Joining us to talk about these topics and more
text: from our New York Bureau, John McWhorter, Manhattan Institute senior fellow on Public Policy. E.R. Shipp also joins us. She is professor of journalism at Hofstra University and she joins us from the campus there in Hempstead, New York. And Glen Loury, professor of economics at Brown University joins us from member station WRNI in Providence, Rhode Island.

speaker_label: Joining us to talk about these topics and more
text: All right folks, here is something that clearly people were looking to hear. And I was surprised, John McWhorter, that I did not hear more about this in the news, quite frankly. For the first time this week the President announced that he expects to turn over most of Iraq to what he deemed the newly trained Iraqi troops by the end of this year, a timetable if you will. This is something that people have been asking about. Again, not the kind of hoopla that I thought would surround this announcement.

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: Well what's interesting is this is really seismic because for the Bush Administration to say something like this, which clearly isn't true. I mean, the Iraqi troops are not going to be ready in anything like that time, shows that they are actually having to acknowledge that something is terribly wrong in Iraq at this point.

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: It's really just a kind of posturing because that's not going to happen by December or, if you ask me, the December after that, but it means that things have gotten so clearly bad, it's not almost a civil war in Iraq right now, it is a civil war depending on what you call it. That we're seeing that something is about to turn around. Even the administration is aware that something needs to be done.

E.R. Shipp, the president acknowledged developments on the ground as being grim in his words, but declared real progress in standing up for Iraqi forces and defending the nation. It was quietly, again, quietly announced in a speech by the president. it was not delivered with the same hoopla that one might expect. Is this and does this speak to what John is suggesting that the White House doesn't totally believe that this is going to work?

Ms. E.R. SHIPP (Journalism Professor, Hofstra University): I think that's very true. If 65 percent of Americans say that the president has no real plan for getting us out of the Iraqi quagmire, then he has to do something. And maybe what he's doing is dreaming. I would sing the song, but I won't. It's (singing) Dream...
I knew you were going to...

So he has to say something, but he says it in a low-key manner knowing that policy wants such as ourselves will pick up on it and broadcast it to the world that he is thinking about a timetable, but as John says, December 31 does not sound feasible at all to think that the Iraqi troops will be able to take over most of the country. We don't even know who the Iraqi troops are, we keep getting different numbers on how many of them are trained, how many of them are insurgents who are giving away...
Yeah.
...troop movements. We have no real sense of control there.

Glen here's the interesting point, as John noted, this probably will not be feasible in assuming that you would literally turn over the country to these troops. Why would a White House that continues of late stumble, make a statement like this. Is it desperation as John suggested?

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: You know it sounds an awful lot like desperation to me. They have to say something, they're taking a terrible political beating over this and what with all the other things that have gone wrong. And when you just step back and take the toll of this horrible fiasco, which has been this intervention in Iraq: our Constitution is frayed, our army is overstretched, our reputation in the world has been tarnished. Xenophobia has been promoted at home. This has been a disaster and I think they're trying to manage the problem as best they can, but unfortunately, the circumstances on the ground militate in favor of a very negative outcome for us over there.

There's something else that may become problematic for the Bush Administration: we heard from the secretary of Health and Human Services this week, a recommendation that Americans start to store canned tuna, powdered milk and other non-perishables under their bed with the prospect of the deadly bird flu outbreak...

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: Why under the bed?
...approaching the United States.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Oh, I'm doing it. Oh I'm doing it.

Here is the question E.R., does this become a Y2K all over again, Chicken Little and the sky is falling or is this just being prudent based on what we saw with Hurricane Katrina and giving fair warning.

All right let's go this way: everybody in America ought to have stuff in their house that they can use in an emergency, but for the secretary of health to tell people to store tuna fish under their bed sounds as ridiculous as plastic tape and duct tape after 911 when people realize that they will be suffocating in a room that they had sealed themselves off on with their tuna fish, I say no. It's stupid.

For my thing, after 911, I started telling people okay, have the tuna fish and the peanut butter, but you don't want to go out that way. You want to go out with ribs and collard greens and friends and good soul music.

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: But there is an incompetence in this country. And read a book about the flu epidemic of 1918-19. If it comes, no one is going to be able to help us; it certainly is not going to be any national administration. So I'm not going to just save tuna. I mean, there are all sorts of things that I like, but it's definitely worth thinking about because you do not want to die of the flu and I fear no one being able to help me. Blowing up in the subway, that's something I worry about, dying of the flu in a room full of tuna fish, is something that worries me.

There's the rub Glen Loury, the idea that if in fact this country were to be infected by the bird flu in the way the influenza took over, as John said, in the early part of this century, it wouldn't matter that you had a week's worth of tuna under your bed.
Why under the bed though?

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: And it's not just a week, it's, we'd need major provisions.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Look, this is too easy to ridicule, I think making prudent preparations for the possibility of an outbreak is sort of the equivalent of getting out of New Orleans when they tell you that the hurricane is coming. We don't want to wait until the last minute to all rush down to the local market and try to fill up our pantry because then the shelves are going to be bare.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: You know, there is something that we can do, I grant you that it really sounds ridiculous and why under the bed, why not the basement or the closet? But the idea that we might begin to get ourselves ready if we're not already for the need to stay indoors for a protracted period of time because of some pandemic, is a reasonable thing, it seems to me.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: MS. SHIPP: But you know what...

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Maybe manhand, yeah...

As I said before, you should be prepared for any of these emergencies by having certain staples on hand. You should have bottles of water, you should have your peanut butter, your tuna, whatever your preference is...
Mm hmmm.
...but you should have that on hand, period. It doesn't matter if we're talking bird flu, terrorist attack...

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: Blackout.
...snowstorm, whatever. That should be the case, but...

Yeah, good luck with that E.R., you live in the North and you can take a look at the grocery stores whenever they announce a big snowstorm and you know what will happen, but one of the things you talked about was a staple and you suggested soul music which takes us to our next question and that is Isaac Hayes raising the ire of the South Park creators, though they've been both kind of playing nice in the press. He has stepped away from a character that many of the new generation only know Isaac Hayes and that's the character of Chef in South Park. We're going to play a little bit from that, this is Isaac Hayes' character in case you don't know what he's about and like. Go ahead, Taylor.
No?
You see children, sometimes a man needs to be with a woman; but sometimes when the loving is over, the woman just wants to talk and talk and talk and talk...

...but a prostitute is someone who would love you no matter who you are or what you look like. Yes, it's true children. That's not why you pay a prostitute, no you don't pay for her to stay, you pay her to leave afterwards.

Okay, so that's just some of the irreverence that people who watch South Park are used to and Chef is one of the recurring characters and one of the craziest characters. And what we have heard from Isaac Hayes, who, much like his prostitute song there, has dealt with some sensitive issues through the years as they parodied many, many things on this show--but he has suggested now that he believes that the show has inappropriately ridiculed religion.

In particular, many people are pointing to the idea that they, in fact, in a recent episode played satire against the Church of Scientology, which Mr. Hayes is a part of. Here's the real question: we can't speak to whether Isaac Hayes should be able to step away, E.R., from what his beliefs are, but do you believe that the irreverence that we've seen in many shows, in particular South Park, starts to cross a line when we talk about these things that heretofore have been untouchable, like religion?

Well, to talk about South Park specifically, it started as a show that grew out of ridiculing religion and sacred iconic figures. So, for Isaac Hayes to suddenly get religion on this, so to speak, is a bit suspicious. They've ridiculed Jesus, they've ridiculed Jews, they've ridiculed a lot of different faith communities on this show.

Now, Hayes said something though, having said that, he said something worth thinking about, particularly as people around the world, particularly in the Middle East and in Africa have been really upset about these cartoon depictions of Muhammad. People are dying around the world because of rioting, this is what Hayes said: religious beliefs are sacred to people and at all times should be respected and honored. As a civil rights activist of the past 40 years I cannot support a show that disrespects those beliefs and practices.
My question is why did it take him so long to come to that conclusion?

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: You know, obviously what really ticked him off was the Scientology part and I wish the man would have a sense of humor. It's one of those where do you draw the line cases. I don't think South Park would be funny if it depicted kicking a pregnant woman in the stomach or something like that, but when it comes to twitting religion, it seems that we're at a point, in Western society at least, where we can be humorous or ironic about such things. And for Hayes to suddenly step away claiming that it's not funny, for example, that this show has a Jesus character, frankly it's primitive. It makes it seem like he hasn't advanced to the late 20th Century and early 21st Century.

Well, Loury, let's allow for people if we can here to change their minds. We should note in December of last year he was asked about the Scientology episode in particular and Isaac Hayes is quoted as saying, "one thing about Matt and Trey," and these are the co-creators of the program, "they lampoon everybody and if you take this 's'-fill in the blank--seriously, then I'll sell you the Brooklyn Bridge for $2.00, I ain't buying it."

Now he is suggesting, as E.R. said and here's a further quote from Mr. Hayes, that he sees "a growing insensitivity towards personal, spiritual beliefs in the media, including the recent controversy over cartoons depicting the prophet Muhammad." Perhaps this is just...

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Let's talk about that...

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: Perhaps this is just a metamorphosis that has occurred in his belief.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Perhaps and perhaps it's a bit of a culture war inside of the South Park TV show.
Or perhaps it's a contract negotiation ploy.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: That's a possibility as well, but I'm inclined to think that it's a great gift of our culture that we are able to engage in this kind of ridicule, criticism, joking, humor. It's a way of letting of steam, it's a way of not taking things too seriously. Everybody doesn't share the same religious beliefs, it's true that religious beliefs should be respected, but it's also true that their pluralistic.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: And for us to be able to get along in civil society with each other, when we have different pluralistic beliefs, requires a certain amount of deference and respect, but it also requires a certain amount of lightening up and being able to laugh at yourself when people are not being invidious or malicious in what they're doing.
All right, let me get...

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: So I don't really se a problem.

Let me get to this quickly with about a minute each for everybody. A parish in Louisiana is looking at hiring a private Texas company to provide security in certain regions. These employees will be deputized to make arrests, carry weapons and they'll dress in the same uniform as do the St. Bernard Parish Sheriff's Department. This is based on the idea that many of the areas are now seeing evacuees come back in and the strapped sheriff's department is not able to police in the way that they would like.
John McWhorter--problem here?

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: Well, no because unfortunately we can talk about why, for example, there might be an uptick in criminality when those evacuees come in. But, for example, in Houston in November and December, the crime, the homicide rate went up 70 percent, five out of 14 of the homicides in Houston were from people who were from New Orleans.

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: And so the fact is that there does have to be a certain kind of measure taken when large numbers of evacuees from New Orleans come in and we don't have to condemn the people in order to admit that that tends to be a problem because of the experiences of those people.
E.R. Shipp, you know what the concern is going to be, that we're going to kind of see this happy policing by junior sergeants who now are given power to wield the big stick.

That may be an issue, but what seems to me more glaring is that the parish we're talking about, St. Bernard Parish, laid off or fired or whatever you want to call it, about two-thirds of its staff and now they're going to hire people to come in at much more money than they were paying their original officers. Why not try to bring back the original officers who know the community, who know the players, and can use the income and the normalization of their own lives? It seems, to me, to be a stupid policy on the basis of that alone.
Glen?

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Yeah, I think this is right, both what John and E.R. have said. That is: security is necessary, let's face it, but that the real issue here is a two-track employment thing where the private company comes in and at $750.00 a day to employ these people and they thing that's a low rate, whereas the full- time guards were making 30 grand a year down there and it has been pointed out some have been laid off.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: I don't know all the logistical details. There's also the issue of whether or not FEMA would provide money to the parish that it could use in that way, but the problem is going to be resentment within the ranks of people who are being paid on very different tracks to do basically the same job.

Well, not just the ranks here, what's surprising to me and I'm a little shocked that no one in this group suggested, historically when we've seen outsiders brought in, in capacities like that as E.R. noted, if you don't know the lay of the land, particularly if you've shipped in from other areas like this, Texas to Louisiana, often there is this sense of occupation.

It's the reason often that there is a residency requirement for police officers--the idea that, you know, you can wield power in a place that you don't live and don't have to answer to in a different way than if you were part of the neighborhood and have to see the guy at the local corner store, at the local movie, your kids go to school together. So it will be interesting to see, outside of the economic, how this all plays out.
All right guys, that does it for this round of the ROUNDTABLE. John, Glen, E.R. thank you very much.
Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. John McWhorter (Manhattan Institute Senior Fellow in Public Policy)
text: Thanks.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya. On today's roundtable, more from President Bush defining his position on terror, and New Orleans mayor, Ray Nagin wants people to rebuild at their own risk.

Joining us today to discuss these topics and more, Glen Loury, professor of economics at Brown University. He's at member station WRNI in Providence, Rhode Island. And from our New York bureau, ER Shipp, professor of journalism at Hofstra University, and Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition.

Welcome, and let's start in Louisiana. Mayor Ray Nagin presented his plan for resurrecting New Orleans. He said residents should be allowed to rebuild anywhere as long as they understand they're doing it at their own risk. He said the city will continue issuing building permits, but warned that low-lying neighborhoods, like New Orleans East and the Lower Ninth Ward, could flood again.

Now, this is in response to an unpopular plan that called for turning low-laying areas into parks or wetlands. But E.R., will this hurt the rebuilding if only some people build in these heavily damaged areas?

Professor E.R. SHIPP (Professor of Journalism, Hofstra University): It has the potential for doing that, sure. There's also the question of what kind of infrastructure there would be in some of these neighborhoods that are more likely to suffer from hurricanes. The season starts pretty soon, by the way. I think the mayor is being a bit irresponsible. It may sound politically correct to tell everybody they can come back and build wherever they want to, but this is an opportunity for New Orleans to rethink the environmental soundness of its plans, to rethink how it wants to reshape the city.

Glen, you are a professor of economics, an economist. I recently went back to New Orleans and there's so many different competing economic interests. There's homeowners, renters, real estate speculators, federal, state, and local government.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Right.
How do those economic interests get reconciled?  And how should they be reconciled when it comes to rebuilding?

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Well, that is the question. I think the mayor is being a bit, sort of, lacking in leadership in not recognizing the need to coordinate the actions of all the parties involved here. And to ensure that people, who don't have otherwise a stake at the table, get represented. The people who were living in rental apartments, for example, who were flooded out, don't have any way really to get back in.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: And in general, these low-income areas, which might not be viable environmentally, nevertheless housed an important part of the city's population and culture. And a way needs to be found to give those people a seat at the table so that they can participate in the reconstruction of New Orleans.
Michael, how do you give people a seat at the table?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, you stop with the publicity gimmicks and you stop with the nonsense. You know, parts of New Orleans are like a ghost town. Are the levees fixed yet?  I want to know. What does it mean to rebuild at your own risk?  This is getting to be like the situation at Ground Zero in New York City. After four years, in New York City, there's still a big hole in the ground and it's become a tourist attraction.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: The ghost town in New Orleans is a tourist attraction. Katrina was a natural disaster, from which we should have learned lessons, and as E.R. suggested, it was an opportunity for imagination, an architectural plan, how to build, where to build, how high to build, the cost of building? What about a new town concept?  There is no imagination here. There is no genius here. All there are seems to be is public hearings where there are constant charges of racism. There's a failure of the human intellect there and political, bold leadership.

Let me move you, Michael, to another topic. In a press conference yesterday, President George Bush said that the decision about when to withdraw all the U.S. troops from Iraq will be made by future leaders, suggesting that U.S. troops could stay in Iraq at least through 2008. Now, the President also defended Donald Rumsfeld.

I think he's done a fine job of not only conducting two battles, Afghanistan and Iraq, but also transforming our military, which has been a very difficult job inside the Pentagon. Listen, every war plan looks good on paper until you meet the enemy. Not just the war plan we execute in Iraq, but the war plans that have been executed throughout the history of warfare. In other words, the enemy changes tactics, and we've got to change tactics, too. And no question that we've had to adjust our tactics on the ground and perhaps the clearest example is in the training of Iraqi security forces.
Now, Senator Dianne Feinstein is calling for Rumsfeld to resign. Michael, is there real pressure behind Rumsfeld to get out of office?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: No. The only pressure for Rumsfeld to get out would have to come from the president, and the president yesterday made a big concession and admission. And that is that we are going to be in Iraq even when he's not president, '08. Look, they might as well stick a fork in his presidency. This guy is done, and so there's no impetus for Rumsfeld to get out. The problem here is that speech, after speech, after speech, after speech, they are not working.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: They have Orwellian properties to them, fear, war is peace, victory over terrorism, sectarian violence. We have fake news in Iraq paid for by the U.S. government. After three years of war, we have an Iraqi parliament that cannot but for 30 minutes, and adjourns. What kind of situation is this?  This is a disaster. Get out!

Yes, but the president isn't going to get out, so we've got to figure out some kind of options. He said in that news conference that if he didn't believe in the war and didn't believe it could be won, he wouldn't have put those kids over there, meaning the soldiers, many of whom are not kids, by the way, particularly with the experience they've had. So he's not going to get out. I don't know that Congress has the will to insist upon anything.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: They don't.
So we're stuck there. We've been there three years, in what was supposed to be a relatively short war. More than 2,300 young people have died and countless thousands more wounded. So we are…

Sorry. E.R., you know, it strikes me that although we are certainly embroiled in this war, it's not the kind of war that some people think about every day. People with families in the military, yes, and people who are looking at policy, yes, but it's not as if every day we're asked to get up and look at car bombs or anything like that. So is that part of the issue here, that we just don't feel it in a visceral way at home?

Sure, but the president took it in a different direction. He said that we're seeing too much of the negative side of the war and not enough of what's going on, the rebuilding of infrastructure, the rebuilding of schools, and all of that. So I notice today, that on television networks, correspondents were going out of their way to try to show how they're trying to do those positive stories, but that is dangerous there.
So it's dangerous for the troops. It's dangerous for the press corps. They can help to shape the image, but the President would rather blame the media for undermining the war effort.

Glen, can you give us some kind of an overview of what a war might cost in economic terms and also political terms if it extends, say, through the 2008 presidency, whoever becomes president in 2008, if it goes on until 2012, what will this do to our country?

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Well, you know, I think Michael Meyers is right. This is a failed policy. We're spending $150 billion dollars a year. We have squandered our good offices with governments around the world. We've inflamed the enemy, as the president is fond of referring to this discontent in the Islamic world. This has been a failed policy.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: And E.R. is right. The president is sticking with it. He is betting the farm on this failed policy and I think the responsibility now falls to the American people who get to go to the polls in November to express ourselves, the scales having finally fallen from our eyes, in opposition to this government and the party that is running it. This is a failed policy, no good for the American people, and we need to say so in no uncertain terms at the polls this November.

Michael, however, although Democrats have been vociferous in criticizing President Bush, a lot of the Democrats gave him the power to proceed with this war. And some Americans, according to polls, are not necessarily that enthusiastic about a Democratic opposition in Congress, so it's unclear which way that will go. Do you think the Democrats are going to gain enough ground to become a true opposition party in the 2006 elections?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: No. You used the word vociferous. I don't think the Democrat Party has been vociferous at all. Maybe one person in the Democrat Party, their so-called leader, chairman, Dr. Howard Dean has been vociferous, but he's the only one. The Democrats beat a quick path away from everything he says.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: No, this Democratic, pusillanimous party is--they are so ridiculous. They are so weak. They are so timid. They are so outrageously un-opposite, un-opposite the GOP, that it's embarrassing for them, and it's embarrassing for anybody who would be motivated to go to the polls.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: So no, this is not just President Bush's war. This is a Congressional war. It's the Congress that continues to fund this war. It's the Congress that continues to have deficit spending, and it's the Congress that continues to empower the president through overwhelming numbers of votes for the USA Patriot Act; and this so-called war on terrorism, this phony war on terrorism. It is Orwellian. I'm sick of it.

All right, well on that note, I'm going to move ahead to another conflict in the Sudan. Darfur, Sudan, has been called a place of genocide, but the New York Times ran an eight-page advertising supplement paid for by the Sudanese government claiming the country has, “peaceful, prosperous and democratic future.” Now, human rights activists are seething and the Sudanese government probably paid close to a million dollars for these ads, should The New York Times, E.R., face any consequences?

Well, that's for its readers and other advertisers to say, I suppose, but The Times is approaching this as strictly a business decision. Somehow, the First Amendment is involved and all of that, but it really does, to borrow Michael's words that he's used a couple of times now, Orwellian, to have the government in Sudan trying to convince the world that it is now a democratic society that is safe for all of its inhabitants. We know that the opposite is very true.
And Glenn, you know, one of the columnists at the New York Times has just been absolutely out there, Nicholas Kristof…

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Yeah.

…criticizing the Sudanese government, so it puts The Times in an especially strange light because one of their editorial employees has been so far out there. You know, can you really separate business and the editorial side when it's a situation this grave?

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Well, I think you should.

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: I mean, I think the free speech argument here is bogus. I mean, the spokesman for the Times is quoted in the newspaper as saying, in accepting this advertisement we do not endorse the politics, trade practices or actions of the country or the character of its leaders. Perhaps, but you do further their ends. Can they not know that? It's impossible that they cannot know that.

And I'm sure that there are other instances where The New York Times and other newspapers have rejected certain advertising supplements, such as this particular one from the Sudanese government. So at some level, someone has to exercise some moral authority; but the rationale this time around is that it was more or less a business decision.
Michael, another topic.
Mm hmmm.

The American Red Cross has supported a lifetime ban on blood donations by men who have sex with men. Now, the organization is reconsidering its position, the Red Cross is prompting the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to do a risk assessment that could reverse a 16-year-old ban excluding any man who has had gay sex since 1977 from ever donating blood. So that means that if you've had gay sex since 1977 you can't give yesterday, today, tomorrow, next week, whenever.
Is this an issue of rectifying undue discrimination or should the ban stay in place, Michael?

This policy is an ignorant as the advertisement for the Sudanese in The New York Times. Look, this is reminiscent of the bias against Haitians in the 80s when they excluded Haitians from giving blood. The safety of the blood supply cannot be based on donors' answers to questions, by the way, about their sexual partners. Beyond that, you cannot exclude the entire segment of the population based on some stereotype or prejudice.

There is people on the down low, there is heterosexuals who are at risk, you get AIDS through unprotected vaginal and anal sex and through the use of (unintelligible) and dirty needles and so the transmission of AIDS is clear. Anybody can be at risk, so the point for me is, is there a reliable blood test? And unless there are reliable blood tests, everybody is at risk. But you cannot single out certain parts of the population based on their sexual practices and what they say their sexual practices are. It's just an ignorant policy and the FDA ought to know better, the courts ought to know better and all the leadership should be revamped and rehauled and just eliminate all that.
E.R., what do you think?

Well, this is one of those vestiges of the hysteria that ran through the country quite rampantly in the 80s when AIDS was just being “discovered.” People feared that you could get AIDS by touching someone with AIDS, by shaking a hand, by sharing a dish, all of those kinds of things.

The blood situation goes back to that crazy period. We've come a long way, so it's about time that we address the exclusion of people as a group. And I think there's a practical side; the blood banks aren't' getting a sufficient supply of blood if they keep excluding entire groups and we'll have a hurricane season and we'll need blood because of the war effort. So, I think this has a practical side also.

Certainly we are in a blood crunch. You mentioned the war, hurricane season; it's a time when there is a great need. Glenn, what should be done, not only to deal with the question of who should be allowed to donate, but how do you generate donations in a time of need like this?

speaker_label: Mr. GLEN LOURY (Professor of Economics, Brown University)
text: Yeah, well, I think we have a case of profiling here of, you know, homosexual profiling and it's subject to all the criticism that you would make of racial profiling or anything else. I think Michael hit on the key point though, you need to have reliable ways of testing the blood supply, you can't be basing the security of the blood supply on people's answers to these kinds of questions. So I think that's the key thing.

So we've talking with Glen Loury who's a professor of economics at Brown University at member station WRNI in Providence, Rhode Island, and also with contributors in our New York bureau: E.R. Shipp professor of journalism at Hofstra University and Michael Myers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition.
Thank you all so much for joining us.
Thank you.
Thank you.

You're listening to NEWS AND NOTES from NPR News.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya. On today's Roundtable, black Republicans try to woo the former head of the NAACP, and anti-Bush rhetoric gets a worldwide audience at the U.N. this week.

Joining us today from our NPR headquarters in Washington is Joe Davidson, an editor at The Washington Post. At member station WRNI in Providence, Rhode Island, Glenn Loury, professor of social sciences and professor of economics at Brown University. And by phone we've got Mary Frances Berry, professor of history at the University of Pennsylvania.

Thank you all for joining us, and I hope that you were all listening to our little discussion with Howard Dean, head of the Democratic Party, and Tara Wall, who's an outreach director for the Republican Party. I want to go to a kind of interesting twist on all of the partisan politics.

Black Republican groups made an appeal this week to persuade African-American voters to support Maryland Lieutenant Governor Michael Steele's bid for the U.S. Senate. He's African-American, he's a former Monk, he has all sorts of interesting bits in his resume.

But they're trying to reach Kweisi Mfume, who just lost in his bid for the Senate to be Steele's challenger, and the appeal is based on race. It says African-Americans should unify and support the black candidate. Professor Berry, what do you think about that?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, here's what I think, Farai. I think that, first of all, it was interesting - the Republican Party's approach is to focus simply on the color of whoever it is and blacks should vote for them.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And one example of how they operate is the choice of who to put on the air. I mean for the Democrats you have Howard Dean. For the Republicans, they have -and people can pick anybody they want to and they have all kinds of people in the Republican National Committee - they go directly to the person who's the African-American outreach, which tells you their thinking.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: The picking of candidates, what the candidates stand for. If black voters do vote for Michael Steele in Maryland it will be because he's black. I don't know if that'll work, because blacks supported Clarence Thomas when he was up for the Supreme Court and most of them did it, even though they didn't agree with anything he stood for, because he was black and they wanted another black person on the Supreme Court.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: So I don't know how far we've gotten away from the idea of we will just focus on, boy, we'd like to have some more black people or not. But we're going to find out in this race. But I'd be surprised if Mfume does support Steele since they differ philosophically. And I don't think he will do it - Mfume will make his decision simply based on race.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And he's known Cardin a long time and they get along and they stand almost in the same position on almost every issue you can think of.

You're talking about the difference between issue-based thinking and skin color-based thinking. How does that parse out, do you think, when people make decisions? I mean is one more important than the other?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, in fact, we've seen - and I've been watching this a long time as I pointed out the Clarence Thomas example - the Condi Rice example. Many black people don't like, politically, where the administration stands and what Ms. Rice has to represent. But most black people that I know say, well, it's nice to have a black person in that job. Somebody has to do that job and it's the first time and she's articulate and whatever, so we're happy to have her there.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: The decisions we make and that blacks make in this election will tell us how far we've come from simply saying we're going to pay attention that we need more black folks, just as women do, for example, when they say, well, we need more women doing that, without regard to what they're doing and whether they're more concerned about issues.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: I have a hunch though that we've moved so far that people will make their judgments based on where people stand. They've had too many examples of how Clarence Thomas turned out in the end and there were people who had supported him. And then when he decided things they said they were sorry and they didn't understand that. So we'll see. But I bet that they will vote for Cardin.

You know, Joe, you're an editor at The Washington Post. This is kind of your turf, a race like this. What do you see or what do you hear in terms of the Cardin/Steele race and how African-Americans are going to make their choices?

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: Well, I think one interesting thing about this organization of black Republicans that is trying to get Kweisi Mfume to back Steele is that they produced a radio ad which was designed presumably to secure black votes for the Republican candidate.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: That ad said, among other things, that Martin Luther King was a Republican, and this is something that historians have said there's absolutely no evidence for. He did not endorse any candidate. They've also tried to link Democrats to the Ku Klux Klan and other things like that.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: And I think that this ad, if it's an example of their strategy, it seems to have backfired, because even Michael Steele issued a statement yesterday basically denouncing the ads. Saying that the kind of flash and burn partisan politics, as he called it, you know, has no place in American politics even though he said the group might have had good intentions.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: And so I think that this is kind of a tale of how not to approach the black voter. And I think that if you want to attach - if a black Republican wants to attract a black voter, that candidate actually needs to go about it in somewhat the way Steele is doing it, and that's not to play up his Republican ties.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: Steele's ads that are running in the Washington metropolitan area as well as across - which of course includes the Maryland suburbs and across the state, makes no mention of the fact that he's a Republican. And he's doing this not just to attract black voters but he's doing it because Maryland is basically a Democratic state.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: But he shows, I think - and his ads, by the way, are very polished, very well done ads - and it's quite the contrast to a much more I guess could I call it ham handed approach to trying to say King was a Republican, Democrats are Ku Klux Klan members, or were. That's simply going to turn off the black community.

Professor Glenn Loury, there's a lot of issues on the table when it comes to recruiting the black vote. It's not just skin color, it's also about moral values. And recently there was a story that came out that said that only 2.6 percent of black churches received funds from the administration's faith-based and community initiative.

And the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies conducted the study, said that it's because a lot of black churches don't really have the resources to apply for grants. Now when you come down to one of these - you know, one the bridges between the Republican Party and African-Americans has been this appeal to we have the same moral values. Certainly there is some evidence of conservative values, social values in the black community.
Do you think that kind of where the money is flowing will have any impact on this race?

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: No, I don't. I think we have to keep our eye on the ball here. I mean, you know, there's a distinction between politics, which is about how the country's going to be governed, what the major policies are going to be, are we going to have healthcare for people who need it, are taxes going to be cut or are they going to be raised to provide social benefits and the rest.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: And then there's being proud of an African-American who has made it in life. You know, Condoleezza Rice, God bless her, or Michael Steele for that matter. What the Republican Party stands for, all you have to do is look at their coalition. Look how they get themselves elected around the country.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: Gun lobbies, anti-tax, Christian right. Not that African-Americans are not Christians, but I'm saying the policies that they have been following at the national and at the local level have definitely been deleterious to the interests of African-American people.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: I'm talking about the death penalty. Who gets executed in this country? The jails are overflowing of young black men in this country. We've basically given up on helping people in terms of any kind of long-term commitment to income support. Those are the issues that really matter.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: And from African-Americans there can be no doubt but that ideology of the Republican Party is not in our interest. And therefore when some black Republicans get the assignment of ginning up the black vote for their candidates, they can't do anything else but make these silly appeals to some kind of racial loyalty, which really hasn't got anything to do with anybody's bottom line.

Glenn, let me just ask you a personal question. You were conservative and then became - I don't even know what you would call yourself now. A liberal, libertarian, freethinker, whatever you want to call yourself. How did you think before about these issues?

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: Well, you know, I'm glad you asked me that. I mean even though the show is not about me. But I'll just take this moment to say...

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: Explain yourself.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: No. I mean I was on this moral trip. It was about unwed babies and it was about black-on-black crime, and it was about how come our kids can't study harder and why can't we help ourselves. Well, of course, we can help ourselves and that's true. But that, in my past I think, I exaggerated way out of proportion relative to the kinds of things that I was just saying, which is what politics about.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: And the problem here is that the moral conversation is really a private, African-American, communal, civic kind of conversation. It should be in the church basement. In front of a microphone talking to America we should be talking about our common public life. And I just woke up to that some time in the mid-1990s.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: And look at what these conservatives and neoconservatives have wrought. I mean I'm lucky I jumped the ship before these guys sailed off to Iraq.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And, Farai, in fact Loury and I had some exchanges during that period...

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: We did?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: ...past. And I used to try to tell him, but he wouldn't pay any attention to me, that it was a both/and problem, not an either/or problem.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: Right.
It probably sunk in when he wasn't even, you know, thinking about it.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Yes.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: You planted a seed, Mary.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Yeah. And then the other thing is - I wanted to point out is as I go around the country, when I speak anywhere Republicans send somebody and they have a whole bunch of leaflets to hand out with that same argument about how Lincoln was a party of blacks and he freed us and the Klan did this. They hand that out. That's their message everywhere. And then they have one other argument. We're the moral party, and we're against same sex marriage. And then they make these two arguments and we have black candidates, and then they sit down.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: So wherever you go in the country where you find people campaigning, that's what you're hearing them say.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: But, you know, and on this point of black candidates, Tara Wall talked about the black candidates running for statewide office in Ohio, Pennsylvania and Maryland, and how the Republican Party is trying to recruit candidates. You know, the Joint Center in another report - and by full disclosure let me add that I once worked for the Joint Center - it said that this year there are only seven black Republicans running for Congress. And that's down from a high of 24 in 1994.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: So why this drastic decline if the Republican Party is really out there trying to recruit black candidates as it claims?
Well, we'll see what happens with the three candidates who are still in the game. But I want to turn to the United Nations. It's kind of like, you know, Fourth of July, a lot of fireworks.

First, the president of Iran told the general assembly, by causing war and conflict, some are fast expanding their domination. And then President Hugo Chavez of Venezuela followed by proclaiming, the devil came here yesterday.
But the president also got some backing yesterday surprisingly from Congressman Charlie Rangel, who said this.

But you don't come into my country, you don't come into my congressional district, and you don't condemn my president. If there's any criticism of President Bush it should be restricted to Americans, whether they voted for him or not. And I just want to make it abundantly clear to Hugo Chavez or any other president: Don't come to the United States and think because we have problems with our president that any foreigner can come to our country and not think that Americans do not feel offended when you offend our chief of state.
Joe, you know, Charlie Rangel has not necessarily been known as a huge fan of President Bush. Why do you think he made these statements?

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: Well, you know, Charlie Rangel is definitely a very proud American, a proud Korean War veteran, and he stands up for his country.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: I think though that, as I'm sure you realize, the United Nations is considered international territory. It happens to be in the United States, but it's considered international territory. And so I think it - I don't think that Charlie Rangel, while he certainly has his right to condemn whatever he wants in terms of what's said there, would want to be in the position of saying that international leaders can only say A, B, or C, and can't say X, Y, and Z, when they are addressing a forum at the United Nations.

speaker_label: Mr. JOE DAVIDSON (Editor, The Washington Post)
text: Now clearly the remark by Chavez took a lot of people by surprise, you know, even people who are critical of the United States. And certainly in the United States Congress few people can be more critical of George Bush than Charlie Rangel. There's no question about that. But at the same time, I doubt very much that he would want to restrict the right of anybody, any world leader, to say what they think at an international place, which is the United Nations.

Prof. Berry, what about the applause? Apparently, according to news reports, there was sustained applause for all of these remarks about George Bush as the devil. What does that say about our relationship to the rest of the world right now?

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Well, it says what the Pew opinion poll research shows us about what people around the world think of us. People around the world, by and large, like America and they want to come here, if they can; move here, if they can, in most places. Not the French. They'd rather stay at home and eat croissant and drink café au lait.
The cheese is very good there.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: They want to move here, but they don't like our government and they don't like our policies, and they think we behave inimical to our values. And Chavez, while he was criticizing Bush - and they liked that, the people who applauded. He was funny too, and they liked that. So that he was bashing and he was saying things that they wished they could say. But they then feel they were operating from a position of weakness. They don't have oil or power or the volubility or - and so he was saying what reflected what they thought.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: And so that's why they were applauding. And he was - besides, he was less boring than the president of Iran, who's kind of boring.
I guess it's a popularity contest.

speaker_label: Professor MARY FRANCES BERRY (Professor of History, University of Pennsylvania)
text: Yeah!
Glenn, what do you make of all this?

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: Well, no, it's not a popularity contest. The United States is unpopular in the world in many places because of the things that we are doing in the world in many places.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: The war in Iraq is unpopular in many places in the world. It looks like unilateral, high-handed preemption, which is what it was. The war in Lebanon is unpopular in many places in the world. Our un-variable support for Israel, up and down the line, is unpopular in many places in the world where people see the plight of the Palestinians.

speaker_label: Professor GLEN LOURY (Professor Social Sciences and Economics, Brown University)
text: So while Hugo Chavez was vituperative and incendiary, and disrespectful in the way in which he referred to the president of the United States, he nevertheless was articulating a critique which is very widely held by peoples in the world. And the question is whether or not we're just going to be so arrogant that we're not going to listen to that critique and try to think about what we're doing as a country that is really ultimately redounding against our interests by alienating people who really ought to be our allies in what we need to accomplish together in this world.
Well, we're going to have to leave it at that. And I just want to say, vituperative - a good SAT word for all our listeners under the age of 18.

We've been talking with, in Providence, Rhode Island, Glenn Loury, professor of social sciences and professor of economics at Brown University. In Washington, D.C., Joe Davidson, editor at The Washington Post. And Mary Frances Berry, professor of history at the University of Pennsylvania. She joined us by phone.
